expected_evidence: Geological: sediment/varve records of glacial Lake Agassiz-Ojibway outflow routes (St. Lawrence vs. Mackenzie/Arctic pathways) with datable flood horizons
Geological: freshwater signal (reduced salinity, oxygen-isotope excursions) in North Atlantic and Arctic marine cores near 12.9 ka
Astronomical/ice-core: Greenland ice-core (GISP2/NGRIP) layer-counted chronologies and dust/isotope records bracketing YD onset, used to cross-check radiocarbon ages

Material: radiocarbon dates from North American archaeological and paleoecological sites falling on the ~12.9 ka radiocarbon 'plateau', producing wide/overlapping calibrated age ranges (the core 'dating-uncertainty' signature)
Geological: outburst-flood geomorphology (scour, spillway channels) in the Great Lakes/St. Lawrence corridor with associated cosmogenic or luminescence dates
Model_prior: published paleoclimate modeling studies testing sensitivity of AMOC shutdown to meltwater timing/routing, explicitly noting chronological ambiguity
Genetic: population/paleoecological proxy shifts (pollen, faunal turnover) near the YD boundary, though genetic evidence for a specific meltwater trigger is indirect at best
response.rationale: The hypothesis is essentially a historiographic/meta-claim: that the meltwater-pulse trigger for Younger Dryas cooling remains inconclusive because of dating uncertainty. This is a documented, active debate in the paleoclimate literature (Broecker's meltwater hypothesis vs. alternative triggers), and the interval given (~10,950–9,750 BCE) aligns with the accepted radiocarbon-cal BP window for YD onset, which is precisely the period where a well-known 14C 'plateau' causes wide calibration uncertainty — this is itself the mechanism named. Given no fixed period label was supplied, I map the interval to the 'younger-dryas' period row, where geological (0.65) and astronomical/ice-core (0.7) detectability are comparatively high, since layered ice cores, varves, and marine/lake sediment cores from this era are well preserved and routinely sampled. Material archaeological dating evidence (0.35) is moderate — consistent with the very radiocarbon-plateau problem the hypothesis describes. Textual (0.0) and linguistic (0.05) evidence are essentially impossible this far back, and oral tradition/iconographic evidence (0.1) is negligible, as expected pre-writing. Because the core evidence types needed (geological stratigraphy, ice-core chronology, radiocarbon dating records) have moderate-to-good preservation/detectability and this debate is in fact well attested in existing paleoclimate scholarship, absence of a definitive resolution is better explained by genuine scientific ambiguity (the stated 'inconclusive' status) than by evidence having failed to survive. A low-detectability explanation for silence is not strongly needed here, though the material/archaeological dating channel's moderate score does partly account for why site-level 14C chronologies remain contested.
